title: Consider Shrinking the Change
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article proposes a counterintuitive change-management tactic: instead of always leading with the full scope of a transformation, leaders can deliberately shrink the change to lower the psychological cost of starting. The piece lays out three concrete levers -- narrowing the time horizon, reducing the number of things changing at once, and lowering the bar for the first step -- as ways to make a threatening shift feel safe and doable. It closes with the framing that big change triggers fear while small steps trigger action.
points: Shrinking the time horizon of a change -- days or weeks instead of a full roadmap -- makes it feel less threatening.
Narrowing the surface area of change to one or two initial projects reduces the psychological cost of starting.
Lowering the bar for the very first step, making it easy and painless, gets people moving before adding the next step.
The core claim: big change triggers fear, small steps trigger action.
quotes: It’s not that they avoid speaking about the change or articulating the big picture, but they start by shrinking the change.
Small, bounded change feels more possible, less risky, and more within people’s control. Making the change feel smaller lowers the psychological cost of starting.
When team members learn what they have to accomplish in the next few days or weeks, the change becomes less threatening and more actionable.
Lastly, leaders can lower the bar for participation by making the first step easy.
Those considering shrinkage should remember this: Big change triggers fear. Small steps trigger action.
